introduction: Today we celebrate the Most Holy Body and Blood of Christ. Melchizedek, priest of God Most High, offers bread and wine. Paul hands on what he received: on the night he was betrayed, the Lord Jesus took bread. In the Gospel, Jesus takes five loaves and two fish, blesses them, breaks them and feeds the multitude. In many places, a procession with the Blessed Sacrament follows Mass. Let us adore Christ, who feeds us with himself.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, Christ gives us his Body and Blood as our food. Let us bring our prayers to the Father.
intentions: For the Church: that the Eucharist may be the source and summit of her life. Let us pray to the Lord.
For priests: that they may celebrate the Eucharist with faith and love. Let us pray to the Lord.
For the hungry of the world: that we may give them something to eat, as Jesus asked his disciples. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who cannot be at Mass, the sick, the housebound and prisoners: that Christ may come to them. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may adore Christ in the Blessed Sacrament and recognize him in our neighbor. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord Jesus Christ, you feed us with your Body and Blood. Help us to adore you in this sacrament, and to share our bread with the hungry. You live and reign for ever and ever.

reflection.title: You give them something to eat
reflection.body:
The first reading tells of a mysterious figure. After a battle, Abram is met by Melchizedek, king of Salem and "priest of God Most High," who brings out bread and wine and blesses him. The psalm takes up his name: "You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek." The Church has long seen in Melchizedek a figure of Christ, the eternal priest, and in his offering of bread and wine a sign of the Eucharist.

Paul gives us the oldest written account of the Last Supper. He hands on what he received: "the Lord Jesus on the night in which he was betrayed took bread." Jesus said, "This is my body, which is broken for you. Do this in memory of me." And of the cup: "This cup is the new covenant in my blood." Paul adds: "For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes."

In the Gospel, a great crowd has followed Jesus to a deserted place. As evening comes, the Twelve suggest sending the people away to find food. Jesus surprises them: "You give them something to eat." They have only five loaves and two fish. Jesus has the people sit down, then "He took the five loaves and the two fish, and looking up to the sky, he blessed them, broke them, and gave them to the disciples." Everyone eats and is satisfied, and twelve baskets are left over.

The words took, blessed, broke and gave are the words of every Mass. Jesus feeds us with himself. And he says to us, as to the Twelve: you give them something to eat. Those who receive the Eucharist are sent to feed others.

If there is a Corpus Christi procession, take part. This week, spend time before the Blessed Sacrament, and then find a way to feed someone who is hungry.
